pages.title: The Struck Leaf of the Rib Crypts
pages.by: Copied from the niche-book of the Order's lesser house in the Rib Crypts, leaf the ninety-seventh, the strike and the later hand kept as they stand.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] Written to the earlier bible, before the Names and Feel sections; not yet revised (the thing she asked to be forgotten is still written, not withheld).

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The Niche-Book of the Rib Crypts[/color][/font_size]
Leaf the ninety-seventh. The Laying of the lower wall, under the Weeping Rib, in the year of the Breath nine hundred and sixty-one by the Count, the walls standing at their count. Set down by the archivist of this lesser house, by the Warden's leave, the Tallier holding the lamp.

The Rule of this house is the Rule of the Nine. Nothing is laid nameless. Nothing laid is unlaid. What is written in the book is read at the Feast, and what is read at the Feast is counted, and what is counted is kept. The archivist writes these three clauses at the head of the leaf, as the Rule requires, and asks the reader to hold them in mind through what follows, because the leaf keeps the first and breaks the second, and the archivist has been unable to do otherwise.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The entry, as it was made[/color][/font_size]
[s]Niche the fortieth of the lower wall, being the reliquary, the box of bone with the lid of the same. Laid therein: Sister Un[/s][ … ][s], of the Tithed of the Cheek, received under the Rule as a sister of this house though not of the Nine, by the Warden's word. Her frame, told on the cord at the washing: two hundred and four. Root six. Open. Her number in the Great Count: three thousand four hundred and eighty. Anointed at every joint. Laid facing the stair. Her name said once over the lid by the Warden and once by the Tallier and once by the archivist, as is done.[/s]

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The reason for the strike[/color][/font_size]
That the entry above is struck by the hand that made it, on the same night, with the Warden's leave given before witnesses, and that the reason be written in full so that no brother after shall take the strike for a copyist's error and restore the line.

I. That she went down. Let that be written first, because it is the reason the Warden received her, and the reason she asked what she asked. In her forty-first year she went down the knee-high stair under this house, below the lowest hall, below the lamps, into the body, alone and unsent, and she was gone eleven days by the Tallier's count, and she came up. No Tithed had gone down and come up before her. The Warden has caused this to be written, and does not permit the archivist to write what she said of it, except one thing, below.

II. That she was heard. The Warden questioned her at the grate on the twelfth day. She said that below the halls the ground is warm, and that it counts, and that it knows the count of this house better than this house knows it. And she said that while she was below she heard her name said. Not called. Said, as a brother says the name of a bone he is setting in its place.

III. That she asked. On her bed in her sixty-third year, before the Warden, the Tallier, and this archivist, she asked three things. That her name be not written in the book. That her number be not kept in the Count. That no brother say her name at the Feast, nor at the lid, nor on the stair, nor anywhere above the ground or below it. She said: what is not named cannot be set in its place. She said: I have been set in a place once already, and I would rather be forgotten than fetched.

IV. That the Rule was read to her. Nothing is laid nameless. She said she knew the Rule. She said she had carried a lamp at thirty Feasts. She asked again.

V. That the Warden ruled. The Rule binds the Laying, and the Laying is done rightly or it is not done. Therefore she was washed, told on the cord, anointed, numbered, laid and named, in full, with every clause kept, so that the Mother received her as the Mother receives all. And that done, the Warden gave leave for the entry to be struck, and her number to be set outside the Count, and her name to be unsaid at the Feast, so that her asking also was kept, in full. The Warden said: the Rule says nothing is laid nameless. It does not say the name must afterward be kept. The Tallier asked that his doubt be written. It is written.

VI. That the strike was made so as to leave the first stroke of her name legible, two letters, because the archivist's hand would not do otherwise and the Warden, seeing it, let it stand. The archivist records that this was not asked for and is not covered by the leave given. It is what was done.

VII. That the Count of this house stands, after the strike, two hundred and four fewer than the bones laid in it this year, and that the Tallier has carried the difference up to the Ninth Stair as an open count, and been told to carry it still.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Added below the rule-line, in another hand[/color][/font_size]
Set down by the archivist of the Rib Crypts in the year of the Breath one thousand two hundred and eight by the Count, at the Feast of the Laying, by the Warden's order, the lamp held by the sweeper.

At the count of the lower wall the reliquary of the fortieth niche was found empty. The lid was in its place. The seal of the Warden who laid it was whole, and the seal is cut in this book and was matched. The dust upon the lid lay unbroken. Within there was no bone, no grit, no dust of the kind that is the Mother's, nor any dust at all. The box held nothing and had been holding nothing, by the look of its inside, for longer than any brother here has lived.

The Tallier counted the lower wall and found it fewer by two hundred and four than the Feast before. He counted again. The count stood. It is the only fall in the chronicle of this house, and the Warden has ordered it entered with thanks, as the Rule gives thanks for the fewer, and the Warden has ordered that it be entered also that no brother gave thanks aloud.

No brother opened the box. The archivist has questioned every brother of this house and every sweeper, and the carters who bring bone from the Cheek, and has found no hand that opened it, and sets down that he looked for one with care and for a long while, because he would rather have found one.

The pilgrims who pass through the lower hall touch the lid for luck, and have done so since before the leaf above was struck. They call her Sister Un, from the two letters that can be read. It is not her name. The archivist has not corrected them and will not. He records their custom here because a thing so called is not nameless, and the Rule is thus kept, after a fashion.

The box has since been carried down the knee-high stair by the Warden's order, to be set below the lowest hall, where she went. It rested one night on the road at the milestone above the Weeping Rib. The sweeper reports that no dust has settled where it rested, and that he has swept there daily since to be sure.

The Warden has asked the archivist to write a finding. The archivist writes that she asked to be forgotten, and that the Rule was kept, and that she was obeyed. The archivist does not write by whom.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— the strike stands; the leaf is not to be scraped[/color][/i][/right]
